Last year my scholarship file sat at the district welfare office for two months. I'm Vishal, and I needed that money to pay my hostel fees.
On my fourth visit, the clerk leaned back and said, "Files like this move quicker if you add something, you know. Chai-paani." He smiled like it was a joke.
My stomach dropped. The fees were due in a week. For a moment I actually reached for my wallet.
Then I called my friend Ayesha, who's studying law. She said, "Don't. Check the scheme's official timeline online, write down the date and his words, and file a grievance on the portal. Keep screenshots."
I did all of it that night. I also wrote a polite letter to the district officer, with a copy for my records.
Nine days later, the money came. The clerk never looked at me again. I kept every screenshot, just in case.

qa.a: It sat at the district welfare office for two months.

Student welfare officer's note, Tuesday.
Yusuf, 21, final-year student, came to me with his classmate Karthik. Yusuf's degree certificate had been "pending" at the university's records section for six weeks. His job offer in Pune requires it by the end of the month.
He said a staff member there told him, "It's a busy season. Some students help the process along." Yusuf understood this as a request for money. He looked frightened and said, "If I don't get it, I lose the job."
I told him he was right not to pay, and that we would use the official route. We wrote down exactly what was said, when and by whom. I emailed the registrar's office, copying the grievance cell, with his application number and deadline.
Next step: I will follow up tomorrow and, if needed, escalate to the Dean. Karthik offered to go with Yusuf to collect the certificate.

I need to tell someone, and you're my sister.
The café is ready, except the fire safety certificate. The inspector came, looked around for five minutes, and said the papers would take "six to eight weeks, unless we find a faster way." Then he waited.

I was twenty-five, opening my first repair shop in Kanpur. The clerk at the municipal office said, "Three months. Or three days, if you're sensible." And I was so tired. Rent was running. My father kept saying, "Just pay, beta, everybody does."
I had the money in an envelope in my bag for two days. I kept telling myself it was tiny, that it didn't matter, that the system was the problem, not me.
Then a customer, a retired teacher, noticed my closed shutter. He said, "Every small envelope keeps that clerk in business." It stung, because it was true.
So I applied online, logged every call, and wrote to the zonal officer. It took five weeks, not three days. I lost money. But I don't regret it.

Leela, twenty-five, three months into her first government job, was told by the senior clerk, "Everyone here takes a small 'tea share.' You'll get yours on Friday. Just sign where we tell you."

Karthik Sir, a section officer close to retirement, found her there one evening. "They did this to me too, in 1994," he said. "Keep a diary of every file and every instruction. Refuse politely. If they threaten you, go to the vigilance officer. I'll come with you."
Leela opened a notebook that night.

In Istanbul, Selin, twenty-five, had been waiting eight months for the municipality to approve the ramp outside her grandmother's building. Her grandmother used a wheelchair and hadn't left the flat since winter.
Every call ended with, "It's in process."
Her friend Sofia, a journalist, said, "File a formal information request. Ask exactly where the application is, who has it, and what the legal time limit is."
Selin wrote it that night, calmly and clearly, and submitted it online. She printed a copy and kept the reference number.
Three weeks later, a reply came: the application had been sitting with one department, past its legal deadline. Two days after that, an engineer called. "We'll start next Monday."
When the ramp was finished, her grandmother rolled out into the sunlight for the first time in months and held Selin's hand.

"I'd like to file an RTI application," she said. "About the drain repair sanctioned last year: how much was sanctioned, which contractor, and why the work hasn't started."

Dear Ujjwal,
You asked how we finally got Dadu's pension restarted. Here's how, in case your family ever needs it.
His pension stopped in March because of a "verification issue." We went to the office five times. Each time, a different clerk said, "Come next week."
So I stopped arguing. I wrote a formal complaint to the pension office, listing every visit, date and name, and his pension number. I sent it by registered post and kept the receipt. Then I filed an RTI asking the status of his file and the reason for the stop.
It took six weeks. The reply said a form had been misfiled. They fixed it, and paid the arrears.
Dadu cried when the money came. Not because of the money, he said, but because someone had listened.
The secret, Ujjwal, is copies, dates and patience.
Chinmay

In Lagos, the pothole at the corner of Emeka's street had been there so long that children named it "the Lake." Emeka, twenty-six, had written to the local council once, years ago, and heard nothing. Now he just drove around it and said, "This is Nigeria. Nothing changes."
His neighbour Vera, a nurse, had different ideas. She set up a street group chat, collected photos from twenty households, and sent a joint letter every two weeks to the council, copying a local radio station.

Emeka stood on the new surface, stamping his foot. Vera laughed. "Still think nothing changes?"

Today was the scariest and best day.
Uday's little dog, Toffee, ran out of the park into the market. We ran after him and got lost.

passage:
In the small town of Hosur, Manjula, seventeen, was riding her scooter to her aunt's house with her cousin Pallavi on the back when a police jeep stopped them at the crossing.
"Licence, RC," the officer said.
Manjula's mouth went dry. She found her licence, but the RC wasn't in the seat compartment. Pallavi whispered, "Let's just say sorry and go."
Manjula shook her head. She said calmly, "Sir, I have my licence. The RC is at home. May I call my father to bring it?"
The officer nodded. Manjula called Appa, who came on his cycle in ten minutes with the papers. The officer checked everything and let them go with a warning to always carry the RC.
Riding away slowly, Pallavi said, "You were so calm." Manjula laughed shakily. "I wasn't. I was pretending really hard."

qa.q: Who brought the RC?
qa.a: Manjula's Appa came on his cycle in ten minutes with the papers.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when her mouth went dry?
qa.a: Manjula felt nervous and anxious, especially when the RC wasn't in the seat compartment.

qa.q: Why was Manjula's choice better than Pallavi's idea?
qa.a: Staying polite, being honest about the missing RC and calling her father to bring it resolved the stop properly instead of trying to slip away.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt watching her cousin?
qa.a: Pallavi was probably nervous too, and impressed by how calm Manjula seemed.

grounding: In a small town, a teenager stopped by police stays calm and polite, admits a missing document and calls a parent to bring it.

Pankaj, twenty, was at the tea stall when a scuffle broke out between two groups near the bus stand. His friend Sachin had only been standing close by, but when the police arrived, they took him along with the others.
Pankaj's heart raced. He wanted to shout that Sachin was innocent. Instead, he remembered the legal-awareness session at college.
He walked up to the officer and said quietly, "Sir, may I know why my friend is being taken? And which police station? I'd like to inform his family."
The officer, surprised by his calm, told him the station and the reason: they were questioning everyone present.
Pankaj called Sachin's father immediately and, on the way, called the legal aid helpline number he'd saved from the session. A volunteer lawyer met them at the station.
Sachin was released that evening after giving a statement. "You didn't argue," he said to Pankaj. "That helped."

qa.q: What did Pankaj ask the officer?
qa.a: He asked, "Sir, may I know why my friend is being taken? And which police station? I'd like to inform his family."

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he wanted to shout?
qa.a: Pankaj felt panicked and protective of Sachin, but he chose calm instead.

qa.q: What made Pankaj's response protective?
qa.a: He calmly asked for the reason and the station, informed Sachin's family, and got a legal aid lawyer involved, without arguing.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel about Pankaj afterwards?
qa.a: Sachin seems grateful and relieved, noticing that Pankaj's calm helped.

grounding: A young adult calmly asks why a friend is taken, informs the family and contacts legal aid, showing that knowing basic rights without arguing is protective.

subtopic: Law and police interaction
passage:
"Excuse me, Yamini Ma'am, can I ask something?"
"Of course, Jyoti. That's what this workshop is for."
"If the police take someone for questioning, do they have to say why?"
"Yes. A person who is arrested has to be told the reason. They can inform a family member or friend, and they have the right to speak to a lawyer."
"Even if the police are angry?"
"Especially then. Stay calm. Don't argue or resist. Just ask, politely, 'What is the reason?' and 'May I call my family?' And ask for a lawyer."
"What if they say no?"
"Remember names and times. Your family can contact a legal aid centre or a senior officer."
Jyoti wrote it all down. "My brother was taken last year and we didn't know any of this. We were just scared."
Yamini Ma'am nodded gently. "Now you know. Knowledge helps you stay calm."

qa.q: Who is running the workshop?
qa.a: Yamini Ma'am is running the workshop.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she mentioned her brother?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a leftover fear and helplessness from last year, when her family didn't know their rights.

qa.q: What does Yamini Ma'am advise, and why is it protective?
qa.a: She advises staying calm, asking the reason politely, asking to call family and for a lawyer, and noting names and times, which protects without escalating.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's family have felt last year?
qa.a: They were scared and confused, not knowing what they could ask or who to contact.

grounding: At a workshop, a young adult learns the basics of an arrested person's rights and how to use them calmly without arguing.

subtopic: Law and police interaction
passage:
When my friend Anirban was taken to the police station after a bike accident last year, I was the only one with him. I'm Rehana, and I was twenty.
My first instinct was to scream at the officers. He wasn't even driving; the other biker had crashed into him. But I remembered a college session on rights.
I asked, calmly, "Sir, is he being arrested, and on what grounds?" The officer said they were recording statements. I asked, "May he call his family?" They let him.
I also called the legal aid number from my phone. A lawyer called the station and spoke to the officer on duty.
By night, Anirban had given his statement and gone home with his father.
Looking back, what saved us wasn't shouting. It was knowing what to ask, and asking politely. I still keep that number saved.

qa.q: What happened to Anirban last year?
qa.a: He was taken to the police station after a bike accident.

qa.q: What did Rehana feel like doing at first?
qa.a: Rehana felt angry and frightened, wanting to scream at the officers because Anirban wasn't driving.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that was protective?
qa.a: Rehana calmly asked about the grounds, asked if Anirban could call family, and contacted legal aid, rather than arguing.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt with Rehana there?
qa.a: Anirban probably felt less alone and grateful that his friend stayed calm and knew what to ask.

passage:
Chetan's phone was snatched outside the metro station in Hyderabad. He stood there, stunned, then walked home without doing anything.
"Aren't you going to file a complaint?" his roommate Darshan asked.
"What's the point? They'll make me wait for hours, ask why I was careless, and nothing will happen."
Darshan sat down beside him. "Maybe. But you need the report to block the SIM and for insurance. Let's write everything down first: time, place, what he looked like, the phone's number and IMEI."
They made a list. Then Darshan went with him to the police station. The first constable said to come back tomorrow. Darshan politely asked to speak to the duty officer, who took the complaint and gave them a copy.
Walking back, Chetan said, "I really thought they'd blame me." Darshan shrugged. "Some might. That's why you take someone along."

qa.q: Where was Chetan's phone snatched?
qa.a: Outside the metro station in Hyderabad.

qa.q: Why did Chetan not want to file a complaint?
qa.a: Chetan felt fearful and hopeless, expecting long waits, blame for being careless and no result.

qa.q: What steps helped Chetan file the complaint?
qa.a: Writing down all the details, going with Darshan, and politely asking for the duty officer when the constable refused.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Chetan's reluctance?
qa.a: Darshan understands the fear but sees that the report is needed, so he stays calm and practical, offering to go along.

grounding: A young adult hesitates to file a police complaint about theft, expecting blame and delay, and a friend helps him write details and escalate politely.

"Ankita, you're shaking. What happened?"
"It's that guy from my old college, Mahima. He's made fake profiles with my photos. He's sending messages to my friends saying I'm his girlfriend."
"That's harassment. You need to report it."

passage:
Two years ago, a man snatched my bag on my way home from college in Lucknow. My laptop, my ID, my notes, gone. I'm Deepika, and I didn't want to go to the police. I was sure they'd say, "Why were you walking alone so late?"
My friend Divyansh said, "We're going. Together. Now."
At the station, the first officer said, "Come tomorrow. It's late." I wanted to leave. Divyansh said politely, "Sir, could we speak to the SHO?" We waited forty minutes. The SHO took the complaint and gave me a copy.
Later, when nothing happened for a month, I wrote to the district legal aid office, with the complaint number. The investigating officer called me the following week.
The bag never came back. But the complaint helped me get a new ID, and it made me braver. Looking back, the fear of blame was worse than the station itself.

qa.q: What was in Deepika's bag?
qa.a: Deepika's laptop, ID and notes were in it.

qa.q: What was Deepika afraid of before going to the police?
qa.a: Deepika was afraid of being blamed, sure they would ask about walking alone so late.

qa.q: What steps helped Deepika's complaint go forward?
qa.a: Going with Divyansh, politely asking for the SHO when refused, keeping a copy, and writing to the legal aid office when nothing happened.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt at the station?
qa.a: Divyansh seemed calm and determined, wanting to support Deepika and make sure the complaint was filed.

grounding: A young adult who fears blame hesitates to report a theft, and going with a trusted friend, asking for a senior officer and seeking legal aid help.

"Indu, you know I don't trust the police. After what happened to my cousin."
"I know, Afreen."
"But yesterday at the railway station, I saw something."
"What?"
"A little boy, maybe five, crying near platform three. Lost. People were just walking past. Then this constable came. She knelt down, gave him her water bottle, and asked his name."
"And?"
"She didn't shout for his parents. She took him to the announcement booth, made the announcement three times, and sat with him on the bench, holding his hand, for forty minutes."
"His family came?"
"His mother came running, crying. The constable just smiled and went back to her post."
"So... you've changed your mind?"
"Not about everything. What happened to my cousin was wrong. But I can't say they're all the same anymore."

qa.q: How long did the constable sit with the boy?
qa.a: She sat with him on the bench, holding his hand, for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as she watched the constable help?
qa.a: Afreen felt surprised and moved, seeing kindness from someone she had distrusted.

qa.q: What does Afreen's changed view show about fair judgement?
qa.a: She still holds that what happened to her cousin was wrong, but she no longer paints all officers alike, which is fairer.

qa.q: How might the boy's mother have felt when she found him?
qa.a: His mother was probably terrified and then overwhelmed with relief, running and crying.

grounding: A young adult who distrusts the police sees an officer patiently help a lost child and updates a harsh view, avoiding painting everyone alike.

I used to say "police are useless" at every family dinner. I'm Francis, and I had my reasons: a traffic cop once took money from my father, and I never forgot it.
Then, last winter, driving on the highway near Nashik with my friend Deepika, we saw a motorbike overturned in the fog. A man was lying on the road.
Before we could even stop, a highway patrol car arrived. The officer put out cones, covered the man with his own jacket, called the ambulance and directed traffic in the freezing cold. He talked to the injured man the whole time, calmly. He stayed until the ambulance left.
Deepika said, "That officer probably saved his life." I nodded, throat tight.
Looking back, I still remember what happened to my father. But I don't say "all police" anymore. Both kinds exist.

qa.q: What did the officer cover the man with?
qa.a: He covered the man with his own jacket.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when his throat went tight?
qa.a: Francis felt moved and humbled, seeing an officer act with care after years of believing police were useless.

qa.q: What does Francis learn about judging people fairly?
qa.a: Francis learns that both good and bad officers exist, so it is unfair to paint all police alike.

qa.q: How might Deepika see the officer's actions?
qa.a: Deepika sees them as life-saving, and seems grateful and impressed.

grounding: A young adult with a harsh view of police sees an officer patiently help an accident victim and learns not to paint everyone alike.

Senior teacher's note, Class 5 trip to the zoo, Thursday.
During the afternoon, Ujjwal, ten, wandered off near the aviary. Our new teacher, Amandeep, 24, who had told me that morning that police "never help anyone, only trouble people," was the one who noticed he was missing. She panicked.
We approached a police officer at the zoo gate. He calmly radioed his colleagues, asked for Ujjwal's description and checked the exits. Within twenty minutes, another officer found Ujjwal near the snack stall, crying, and brought him back, crouching to talk to him gently.
Amandeep thanked the officer twice. On the bus back, she said quietly, "I was so sure they were all the same. I was wrong about him."
Next step: I've suggested Amandeep lead a short class talk next week on what to do if lost, including approaching police.

qa.a: Another officer found him near the snack stall, crying.

qa.a: Amandeep felt panicked and frightened for the child.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's changed view show?
qa.a: Seeing the officers help calmly made her realise that not all police are the same, so fair judgement avoids painting everyone alike.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt when the officer crouched to talk to him?
qa.a: Ujjwal was probably scared and then comforted by the officer's gentle way.
